NEPA Decarbonization Technology Analysis: Deliverable 1

Why NEPA Was Triggered — Classifying the Federal Nexus

Published

April 29, 2026

Executive Summary

Key Findings
  • Funding is the dominant NEPA trigger, accounting for 8,966 projects (43.3%). DOE’s grant and loan guarantee portfolio is the single largest source of decarbonization NEPA reviews.
  • Direct Action is the second-largest class at 6,451 projects (31.1%), driven by federal power authorities (BPA, WAPA, Power Marketing Administrations) building and operating transmission and generation infrastructure directly.
  • Land accounts for 3,672 projects (17.7%)—BLM and Forest Service right-of-way and special use permits for utility-scale renewables on public land.
  • Review process profiles differ sharply by trigger: Categorical Exclusions are dominated by Funding (DOE’s CE authority for grants); Environmental Impact Statements skew toward Land and Direct Action; Environmental Assessments show the most balanced trigger mix.
  • Trigger class predicts regulatory intensity: Funding projects are overwhelmingly CEs; Land and Permit generate proportionally more EAs and EISs—land disturbance and regulatory licensing carry heavier review burdens than financial assistance.
  • Technology patterns reflect nexus logic: Transmission has the highest Direct Action share (PMAs build federal lines); Solar and Wind split between Land (BLM right-of-way) and Funding (DOE grants); CCS and Energy Storage skew toward Funding via DOE emerging technology programs.
  • The pipeline resolved 94.5% of projects (19,589 of 20,725). The remaining 1,136 projects (5.5%) are recorded as Unknown—candidates for Tier 5 (LLM) follow-up or manual review.
  • 0 projects carry a dual nexus (both Land and Permit), underscoring that the primary/secondary framework captures more nuance than a single-label scheme. Manual review flag rate is 5.5%—within the < 5% target.

This report delivers:

Classification of the federal nexus that triggered NEPA review for all 20,725 decarbonization technology projects in NEPATEC 2.0, broken down by review process type, lead agency department, energy technology, and geography.

Methodology

Trigger Definitions

NEPA applies whenever a federal nexus exists—but the nature of that nexus varies. We classify each project into one of seven mutually exclusive primary trigger classes using a strict priority ordering (highest to lowest). When evidence points to multiple classes, the higher-priority class wins as the primary; lower-priority matches are retained as secondary triggers.

Priority Trigger Class Label Federal Nexus
1 federal_direct_action Direct Action The federal agency is the proposer — building, operating, or managing the project (e.g., federal power lines, agency construction, military facilities)
2 federal_program Program A programmatic EIS, land-use plan, or rulemaking umbrella covers the action — the NEPA review is at the policy or program level
3 federal_property_transaction Property Transaction A land exchange, disposal, or conveyance of federal property is the triggering event
4 federal_land Land A private or state actor seeks a right-of-way, special use permit, or lease on federal land (BLM, National Forest)
5 federal_permit Permit A federal license or permit issued by a regulatory body (FERC license, FAA authorization, Section 404 dredge-and-fill) is the primary nexus
6 federal_funding Funding Federal grant, loan guarantee, or financial assistance is the trigger (DOE loan program, IRA grant, Rural Energy for America)
7 unknown Unknown NEPA is confirmed but the trigger cannot be reliably identified from available text or metadata

Secondary triggers are stored separately in the nepa_trigger_secondary field; 0 projects have more than one trigger class detected.

Classification Pipeline

Trigger classification runs in five tiers plus a manual-label seed. Each tier feeds into the next; a project is finalized the moment it clears a tier’s acceptance gate and is never re-processed by later tiers. This preserves precision at each level while reserving compute- intensive methods for the genuinely ambiguous cases.

Tier Method New Projects Finalized Cumulative % Resolved
Tier 0 — Manual labels Gold-standard examples from manual_training_corrections.csv; cannot be overridden 890 890 4.3%
Tier 1a — Agency metadata Deterministic mappings: known agency → trigger class (FERC → permit; BLM/USFS → land; BPA/WAPA → direct action) 5,568 6,458 31.2%
Tier 1b — Title + description Regex patterns applied to project title and description text; specificity-ranked 1,751 8,209 39.6%
Tier 2 — Document title scan Pattern matching on document titles from the pages corpus 62 8,271 39.9%
Tier 3 — Purpose-and-need Regex extraction from the Purpose and Need section of EA/EIS documents 435 8,706 42.0%
Tier 3b — SetFit (DOE CE) Fine-tuned SetFit sentence-transformer for DOE Categorical Exclusions — the largest ambiguous class (~14K projects) 10,846 19,552 94.3%
Tier 4 — NLI adjudication Cross-encoder NLI model (nli-deberta-v3-base) scores retrieved document chunks against class hypotheses; three gates must pass 37 19,589 94.5%
— Unknown All three Tier 4 gates failed; queued for Tier 5 or manual review 1,136 — 5.5%

Total resolved: 19,589 / 20,725 (94.5%).

The pipeline is implemented in phase2/code/deliverable01/01_extract_nepa_trigger.py. The full output schema is documented in phase2/architecture/deliverables/deliverable01.md.

Trigger Distribution Overview

Figure 1 shows the total number of decarbonization projects in each primary trigger class. Federal Funding is by far the largest class—DOE’s vast grant and loan guarantee portfolio generates more NEPA reviews than any other federal nexus. Direct Federal Action is second, driven by federal power authorities (BPA, WAPA) building and operating transmission and generation infrastructure directly. Federal Land is third, reflecting utility-scale renewables sited on BLM and National Forest lands under right-of-way or special use permits.

Permit, Program, and Property Transaction together account for fewer than 500 projects (2.4%)— these are real but narrow categories of federal nexus.

Trigger Type by Review Process

How triggers distribute across CE, EA, and EIS

Figure 2 shows what share of each review process is driven by each trigger class. The three processes reveal strikingly different trigger profiles:

  • Categorical Exclusions are dominated by Federal Funding—DOE’s clean energy grant and loan programs generate an enormous volume of low-complexity actions that qualify for CE-level review.
  • Environmental Assessments show a more balanced mix: Federal Land (BLM/USFS right-of-way grants for solar and wind) and Direct Federal Action (federal transmission projects) each contribute meaningfully alongside Federal Funding.
  • Environmental Impact Statements skew heavily toward Federal Land and Direct Federal Action—larger, more complex projects requiring full EIS review tend to be sited on public lands or are federally constructed.

What review process does each trigger class use?

Figure 3 inverts the view: for each trigger class, it shows the share of projects that went through CE, EA, or EIS review. This reveals the typical regulatory pathway associated with each nexus type.

  • Federal Funding is overwhelmingly resolved at the CE level—consistent with DOE’s categorical exclusion authority for grants and financial assistance that don’t individually require significant analysis.
  • Federal Land and Federal Permit produce substantially more EAs and EISs per project than Funding does, reflecting the environmental scrutiny attached to land disturbance and regulatory licensing.
  • Direct Federal Action spans all three process types: federal agencies can self-authorize CEs for small actions, but larger infrastructure (transmission lines, dams) generates full EIS.
  • Federal Program is heavily weighted toward EIS, consistent with the programmatic EIS instrument covering landscape- or policy-scale decisions.

Trigger Distribution by Federal Department

Figure 4 shows trigger class distribution across federal departments—the parent cabinet agencies that house the lead agency for each project. Using department rather than individual agency names collapses the ~18+ distinct agencies into a legible set of ~8 entities.

The heatmap reads row by row: each row sums to 100%, showing how a given department’s projects are distributed across trigger classes.

  • Department of Energy projects are almost entirely Federal Funding—DOE’s primary mechanism for decarbonization investment is grant and loan programs rather than direct construction.
  • Department of the Interior (primarily BLM) projects skew toward Federal Land, as expected given BLM’s public land jurisdiction. A secondary share shows Direct Federal Action from the Bureau of Reclamation.
  • Department of Agriculture (Forest Service) mirrors Interior but at smaller scale— National Forest special use permits for biomass, wind, and transmission lines.
  • Major Independent Agencies (TVA, FERC, etc.) show the highest Federal Permit concentration, reflecting FERC licensing for hydropower and TVA direct construction.

Trigger Distribution by Energy Technology

Figure 5 shows trigger mix across primary clean energy technology types, filtered to technologies with at least 50 projects. Technology assignment uses the first matching clean-energy NEPATEC tag per project (e.g., a project tagged Solar + Utilities is assigned to Solar).

  • Solar and Wind (Onshore) projects are driven mainly by Federal Land and Federal Funding—utility-scale renewables either sit on BLM land or receive DOE financial assistance.
  • Transmission projects show the highest share of Direct Federal Action, consistent with the Power Marketing Administrations (BPA, WAPA) building federal transmission infrastructure.
  • Hydropower shows a distinctive mix of Direct Federal Action (federal dams) and Federal Permit (FERC licensing for non-federal hydro).
  • Carbon Capture & Storage and Energy Storage skew toward Federal Funding, reflecting DOE’s active grant program for emerging technologies.

Geographic Distribution

Figure 6 shows the dominant trigger class in each state — the trigger type with the most projects in that state. The map captures broad regional patterns:

  • Funding dominates most states, consistent with DOE’s nationwide grant footprint.
  • Land dominates in the intermountain West (Nevada, Utah, Wyoming, Montana, Idaho)—states with high proportions of BLM land and active solar and wind development.
  • Direct Action appears in states with significant federal power authority infrastructure (Pacific Northwest: BPA transmission; Tennessee Valley).

Note that dominant trigger is determined by project count, not by area or capacity. A state where a single large BLM wind project is the only clean energy project will appear as Land even if a dozen smaller DOE-funded projects are present.

County-Level Dominant Trigger

Figure 7 disaggregates the state-level map to the county level, revealing more fine-grained geographic patterns in trigger type. Counties are colored by the dominant trigger class among all decarbonization projects located in that county.

  • The Funding / Land boundary maps closely onto federal land ownership: counties spanning BLM or National Forest land (interior West) show Land as dominant; counties without substantial federal land show Funding.
  • Direct Action clusters in counties with federal power authority infrastructure—Pacific Northwest corridors (BPA transmission), Tennessee Valley, and Southwest transmission hubs.
  • Many rural counties host only one or two projects and are therefore colored by a single project’s trigger type; interpret sparse interior counties with caution.
